title: chaiko
tools: c, platformio, kicad, solidworks, react, nodejs

sections.body: an automatic syrup dispenser for my home cafe, built to make barista-level drinks perfectly, every time.

sections.heading: why?
sections.body: I love making specialty drinks for my friends and family. As my home cafe has grown, I wanted a dedicated station for drink mixing, plus an easy way to keep track of my ever-growing list of cocktail and latte recipes. Mixing every drink by hand gets difficult when I'm hosting larger groups, so chaiko was born. Offloading the repetitive work lets me focus on creating recipes, and enjoy my sweet treats even on days when I don't have the time or energy.

sections.heading: how?
body: chaiko pairs a web app with an ESP32-controlled pump system:

items: Web app: built with React, Express, MongoDB, and Node.js to create, manage, and send recipes
Control: selecting a recipe sends its data to an ESP32 over WebSocket, which calculates how much of each syrup is needed and drives the matching pump motors
Food safety: food-safe valves and peristaltic pumps with silicone tubing keep the system food-safe while preserving recipe accuracy
Waterproofing: custom o-rings and gaskets seal every component
Hygiene: a built-in cleaning cycle keeps the system sanitary and easy to maintain
Modes: automatic (recipe-driven) and manual syrup dispensing
Customization: adjustable machine configuration, recipes, and syrups, all editable from the web app

sections.body: a desk-side Spotify controller that shows what's playing, featuring a customizable character who listens along with you.

sections.heading: why?
sections.body: I wanted to view and control my Spotify playback at a glance while studying, without reaching for my phone or computer and getting distracted. Melodie is a cute, functional tool that sits on my desk while I work. Its fully hand-drawn, customizable character 'listens along' to keep me motivated through even the most gruelling study sessions.

sections.heading: how?
body: Melodie runs on a Raspberry Pi:

items: A Python program pulls my listening data from the Spotify API
The current track and album are displayed on the screen using Pygame
Playback and the character's outfits are controlled from a miniature keyboard

sections.heading: what's next?
body: A few features I'd like to add:

items: An RFID reader so tapping different NFC tags plays different albums
Syncing the character's animation frame rate to the BPM of the current song for a more immersive feel

sections.body: design and manufacturing of UWFE's 2026 rear wing.

sections.heading: why?
sections.body: The University of Waterloo Formula Electric aerodynamics subteam designs a new aero package every year. I worked alongside my teammates to design the rear wing for the 2026 season, focusing on increasing downforce and improving mounting stability.

sections.heading: how?

items: Model a concept in SolidWorks
Simulate it in Star-CCM+
Analyze which aspects performed well, then repeat

body: Along the way, we accounted for how the wing interacts with the rest of the car and made sure it could be manufactured. The final components were made from carbon fibre:

items: Wet layups for the airfoils
Resin infusions for the flat panels
Increased rear wing downforce by 15% while improving aerodynamic efficiency

sections.body: a servo-driven gear pump depositor that handles delicate whipped products accurately and consistently.

sections.heading: why?
body: Typical cream depositing solutions, such as piston depositors and pressure tanks, tend to damage delicate whipped products and lack accuracy and consistency. At Apex Motion Control, we designed a new solution: the Apex Motion Servo Depositor.
It uses a gear pump to move product from a hopper to the outlet, which:

items: Preserves the texture of the product
Delivers consistent depositing accuracy
Drive: the gear pump is driven by an Allen Bradley motor, controlled by a Kinetix 5100 servo drive and a Micro850 PLC
Trigger: a pneumatic signal from a pressure switch tells the PLC to start the motor, and pumping stops when the signal goes low
Integration: pneumatic signalling lets the system plug into Apex's existing products, which use pneumatic signals to communicate with peripheral devices, while complying with food safety standards
Modes: one mode where deposit volumes are controlled by an external device, and one for standalone use
HMI: operators can adjust deposit speed, volume, and timing, with user access levels for added security

sections.body: food-grade icing nozzles for cake decorating, designed for use with cobot end-of-arm tooling.

sections.heading: why?
sections.body: At Apex Motion Control, I worked on cake decorating systems that apply the top and side icing (TSI) to cakes of various shapes and sizes. Different cakes need different nozzles to keep the flow consistent, leaving every cake with a smooth, even layer of buttercream.

items: Prototype: modelled nozzle designs in SolidWorks and 3D printed them to test and validate
Production: remodelled successful designs for sheet metal manufacturing, keeping as much of the original geometry as possible so the frosting flow, and the finished decoration, matched the prototype

sections.body: a UR robot script that calibrates robots on conveyor systems equipped with computer vision.

sections.heading: why?
body: Apex Motion Control's BakerBot Quad is a robotic cake decorating system that scans incoming pastries, then decorates them while tracking them along a conveyor. With so many components that need to communicate with each other, a lot of time goes into calibration.
The most notable routine converts a scanned pastry's coordinates from camera coordinates to robot coordinates. Historically, this meant:

items: Physically measuring the offsets between the camera and robot
Scanning and tracking test parts to validate the measurements
Adjusting and repeating as needed

body: That iterative process is extremely time-consuming, especially with several robots along a long conveyor line. I designed a new routine that only needs a part to be scanned once.

items: A part is placed on the conveyor and scanned by a Gocator camera
The UR program fetches camera data via XML-RPC and conveyor encoder data from the PLC via MODBUS
The operator stops the conveyor with the part in front of the robot, then freedrives the robot to the centre of the part
The program combines the camera coordinates, encoder distance, and robot tool coordinates to compute the overall camera-to-robot offset, which is then applied to every future scanned part
Calibration accuracy of ± 2 mm
Reduced camera calibration time by 75%
